lesson.title: Solids Without a Blueprint
lesson.summary: Amorphous solids like glass lack the long-range repeating order of a crystal, so instead of melting sharply at one temperature, they soften gradually over a range as their disordered particle arrangement loosens up.
lesson.body:
An amorphous solid is a solid whose particles are arranged with no long-range repeating order, in direct contrast to the highly ordered lattice found in crystalline solids. The particles in an amorphous solid are still packed closely enough together, and held in place by intermolecular or bonding forces strongly enough, to keep the material rigid with a fixed shape, satisfying the basic definition of a solid. What is missing is the regular, repeating unit cell pattern that a crystal has; instead, the arrangement of particles in an amorphous solid resembles a liquid that has been frozen in place with its disordered, random structure intact, rather than a liquid that has organized itself into a repeating lattice as it solidified.

Ordinary glass, made mostly of silicon dioxide, is the standard example, and comparing it directly to quartz is the clearest way to see the distinction, since both share the same basic chemical formula, SiO2. Quartz forms when molten silica cools slowly enough for its silicon and oxygen atoms to organize into the repeating tetrahedral lattice described in crystalline solids. Glass forms when molten silica is cooled quickly, too quickly for the atoms to settle into that ordered lattice before the material becomes rigid. The result is a solid with silicon and oxygen atoms bonded together in the same basic tetrahedral units as quartz, but with those units connected in a random, irregular network rather than a repeating pattern. This is why glass is sometimes described as a supercooled liquid, though that phrase is a simplification, since glass is mechanically rigid rather than flowing like an actual liquid at ordinary timescales.

The lack of long-range order has a direct and testable consequence for how amorphous solids respond to heating. Because the particles in an amorphous solid are held together by a wide range of slightly different local arrangements rather than one uniform repeating structure, different regions of the material require different amounts of thermal energy to loosen up. As a result, amorphous solids do not melt sharply at a single temperature the way crystalline solids do; instead, they soften gradually over a range of temperatures, passing through an increasingly pliable state before eventually flowing as a liquid. This is exactly what happens when a glassblower heats glass: it does not suddenly turn to liquid at one precise temperature, it gradually softens into a workable, taffy-like consistency over a broad temperature range, which is precisely why it can be shaped.

Other common amorphous solids include rubber, most plastics, and obsidian, a natural volcanic glass formed when lava cools too quickly for mineral crystals to form. In every case, the defining feature is the same: particles that are rigid and fixed enough to count as a solid, arranged without the long-range repeating order that would classify the material as crystalline instead.
